procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of acquittal passed by the Additional Sessions Judge
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The respondent (son of the deceased) filed a criminal revision petition before the Delhi High Court under Section 397/401 Cr.P.C. challenging the acquittal. A Single Judge of the High Court allowed the revision petition, set aside the acquittal, and ordered a re-trial.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants (the originally accused) appealed to the Supreme Court, contending that the High Court transgressed its revisional jurisdiction by reappreciating the evidence and setting aside the acquittal. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's judgment, and restored the trial court's acquittal order.

directions: The judgment of the High Court is set aside.
The order of the acquittal passed by the trial court will stand restored.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court is entitled to set aside an order of acquittal of the Trial Court and order a re-trial in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction under Section 439 of the Criminal Procedure Code, 1973, merely because it disagrees with the trial court's findings of fact.

facts: The appellants were acquitted of a murder charge by the Additional Sessions Judge (the trial court).
The son of the deceased victim filed a criminal revision petition with the High Court challenging the acquittal.
A Single Judge of the High Court allowed the petition, set aside the acquittal, and ordered a re-trial of the case.
law: The revisional jurisdiction of the High Court under Section 439 of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.) is much more restricted in scope than its appellate jurisdiction.

This power should only be exercised in exceptional cases, such as when there is a "glaring legal defect," a "manifest illegality," a "perverse" finding, or a violation of fundamental legal principles that results in a grave miscarriage of justice.
Section 439(4) of the Cr.P.C. expressly prohibits the High Court from converting a finding of acquittal into one of conviction, and ordering a re-trial cannot be used as an indirect means to do so.
Even in an appeal, an appellate court is not justified in interfering with an acquittal merely because it would have reached a different conclusion on the facts.
application: The Supreme Court found that the trial court's decision to acquit was based on its assessment of the evidence of two eyewitnesses.
It concluded that the trial court's assessment was a "possible view" and could not be characterized as illegal or perverse.
The High Court had interfered simply because the judge, after an independent review of the evidence, disagreed with the trial court's findings of fact.

The Supreme Court ruled that a mere disagreement with the trial court's appreciation of evidence is not a sufficient justification for a High Court to interfere with an acquittal in its revisional jurisdiction.
By setting aside the acquittal on this basis, the High Court failed to adhere to the established principles and exceeded the narrow limits of its revisional powers.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court had clearly transgressed the limits of its revisional jurisdiction. A High Court cannot set aside an order of acquittal and order a re-trial merely because it disagrees with the trial court's findings of fact, especially when the trial court's view is a possible one and not manifestly illegal or perverse.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The mere circumstance that a finding of fact recorded by the trial court may, in the opinion of the High Court, be wrong, will not justify the setting aside of the order of acquittal and directing a re-trial of the accused.
obiter: Even in an appeal against an order of acquittal, no interference will be made with the judgment of the trial Court except in rare and exceptional cases where there has been some manifest illegality in the approach to the case or in the appreciation of the evidence or where the conclusion of fact recorded by the Trial Judge is wholly unreasonable.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court is not justified in setting aside an order of acquittal and directing a re-trial in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction merely because it disagrees with the trial court's findings of fact. In this case, the trial court's judgment did not suffer from any manifest illegality; its view of the evidence of the two eyewitnesses was a possible one and cannot be characterized as illegal or perverse. While the High Court may have been inclined to disagree with the trial court's finding on the basis of its own independent scrutiny of the evidence, that does not furnish any justification for interference in revision, which has a much more restricted scope than even an appeal.
legal_tests_applied: The revisional jurisdiction of the High Court under Section 439, Cr. P.C. is to be exercised only in exceptional cases when there is a glaring defect in the procedure or there is a manifest error on a point of law which has consequently resulted in a flagrant miscarriage of justice.

The High Court, when asked to exercise its power of revision from an order of acquittal, should refrain from interfering except when there is a glaring legal defect of a serious nature which has resulted in a grave failure of justice.
The mere circumstance that a finding of fact recorded by the trial court may in the opinion of the High Court be wrong will not justify setting aside the order of acquittal and directing a re-trial.

Even in an appeal against an order of acquittal, interference is not warranted unless the conclusion of fact recorded by the Trial Judge is wholly unreasonable so as to be liable to be characterised as perverse.
The revisional power of the High Court is much more restricted in its scope than its appellate power.
policy_considerations: The statutory scheme of the Criminal Procedure Code confers an unrestricted right of appeal from acquittal only on the State, with limited rights for private complainants. The State, having failed to appeal, cannot apply for revision of an order of acquittal.
The High Court is expressly prohibited under its revisional powers from converting an acquittal into a conviction.

Given the statutory scheme, the High Court's discretionary power of revision against an acquittal should be exercised judiciously and not arbitrarily, informed by tradition and disciplined by system, to prevent it from being used as a substitute for an appeal.
